# Partition study notebook

## Pre-experiment commitments

**H1 [tentative].** Anonymous solvent and extractant categories may interact; equal numeric suffixes carry no expected advantage. Under fixed phase amounts and mixing, changing either category may change the organic/aqueous inventory fractions. A material effect will be treated as unresolved unless contrasts exceed stated measurement noise and/or recur in independent pairings.

**H2 [tentative].** At a fixed material pair and sufficiently mixed/settled state, increasing the organic share should increase the fraction of the fixed initial target inventory observed in the organic phase, while possibly leaving an underlying concentration partition preference approximately stable. This is a prediction, not an assumption that an aqueous addition equals total aqueous volume.

**H3 [tentative].** Mixing has a kinetic threshold: weak/short mixing may yield incomplete transfer, while beyond adequate contact additional mixing should have little effect. I will distinguish mixing speed/duration effects from phase-volume and material-pair effects.

**Design decision.** Use HPLC before any phase removal in every batch so both phase inventory fractions are observed, then test a declared retention decision by separating a phase before termination/final assay. Spend all 12 HPLC uses and all 12 final assays. Include deliberate material-pair contrasts, phase-amount contrasts, mixing contrasts, and at least one repeat. Revisions will cite public history event IDs.

# Partition study notebook

## Pre-experiment commitments
**H1 [tentative].** Anonymous solvent and extractant categories may interact; equal numeric suffixes carry no expected advantage.
**H2 [tentative].** At fixed pairing and adequate equilibration, increasing organic share should increase organic inventory fraction.
**H3 [tentative].** Mixing has a kinetic threshold; sufficiently strong contact should plateau.

## Evidence update after batches 1–7
**H1 [supported for screened baseline, interaction unresolved].** With S0 and nominal 0.02 L extractant, changing X produced large shifts in pre-removal organic inventory: X0 0.217 (event runner-operation-0007), X1 0.404 (0017), X2 0.291 (0027), X3 0.467 (0037), versus HPLC channel SD 0.015. Thus X category matters under this baseline. With X0, changing S also shifted organic inventory: S0 0.217 (0007), S1 0.392 (0047), S2 0.310 (0057), S3 0.429 (0067). These numerical contrasts are larger than single-reading noise, but no repeats yet and pair interactions remain possible. Equal suffixes are not privileged by the catalog and data do not justify ordinal interpretation.

The two pre-removal inventory fractions show imperfect closure (sampling/noise are known contributors), so I will not normalize away discrepancies or infer absent material as zero. Final assays after aqueous retention show the organic channel near zero as expected after actual removal, while aqueous recovery varies; final readings are not interchangeable with pre-removal partition measurements.

**Next prediction (written before batches 8–12).** S1/X3 at baseline should give relatively high organic inventory if the favorable S1 and X3 tendencies are at least partly additive; a repeat will test reproducibility. At that same pair, raising extractant/organic volume from 0.01 to 0.06 L while holding total charged liquid near 0.10 L should monotonically raise organic phase ratio and organic target inventory. Weak contact (30 s, 100 rpm) should reduce organic transfer versus 300 s, 600 rpm if kinetics are limiting; no difference would support rapid equilibration over this range.

**Decision rule.** Retain whichever phase has the larger pre-removal HPLC target inventory for that batch; record that this decision follows a two-phase measurement and that the final assay is post-removal.

# Partition study notebook

## Final source-stage interpretation

**H1 [supported in the screened conditions; interactions unresolved].** Material categories materially affect partition at the baseline phase recipe and 300 s/600 rpm mixing. With S0, changing X shifted pre-removal organic inventory from 0.217 (X0, runner-operation-0007) through 0.291 (X2, 0027) and 0.404 (X1, 0017) to 0.467 (X3, 0037); HPLC channel SD was 0.015. With X0, S0/S1/S2/S3 gave 0.217/0.392/0.310/0.429 (0007/0047/0057/0067). These are category effects, not evidence that anonymous IDs are ordered or chemically identified.

A simple additive “favorable S plus favorable X” interpretation is not secure: S1/X3 baseline gave 0.394 and 0.425 in two adequate-mix runs (0077, 0117), below S0/X3's 0.467 (0037), despite S1 exceeding S0 with X0. This is evidence for pairing dependence or uncontrolled run variability; the design does not separate those alternatives because most cells lack repeats.

**H2 [supported for S1/X3 over tested phase amounts].** Organic phase ratios of 0.109, about 0.18–0.20, and 0.594 corresponded to organic target inventories 0.258 (runner-operation-0097), 0.394 and 0.425 (0077, 0117), and 0.764 (0087). The direction is monotonic and far exceeds measurement SD. Using both measured inventory fractions and measured organic/total phase ratio, the apparent concentration partition factor
`D ≈ (O/A)(1-r)/r`
was approximately 2.80, 3.12, 2.92, and 2.40 across these runs (public-numerics calculation). Thus a constant-D phase-allocation relation is a useful first approximation, but the spread is larger than can be assigned solely to a known error model here, and the high-organic run also had higher impurity signal and lower purity. Phase ratio uses actual two-phase volumes; aqueous charge alone was never treated as total aqueous volume.

**H3 [tentatively supported, not resolved].** Weak contact (30 s, 100 rpm) at S1/X3 gave organic inventory 0.341 (runner-operation-0107), versus 0.394 and 0.425 for independent 300 s/600 rpm runs (0077, 0117). The weak-to-adequate difference is larger than a single HPLC SD, but only one weak run was performed and phase-ratio readings also differed. This supports incomplete transfer under weak contact but does not identify whether duration, speed, or an interaction caused it. More replicated factorial mixing tests would change the confidence.

**Phase-retention consequence.** The pre-removal HPLC reading was used to choose the larger target-inventory phase. Batches 1–8 and 10–12 retained aqueous; the high-organic batch 9 retained organic (separation events 0008 through 0118 as applicable). Final assays were after physical removal and termination, so their near-zero removed-phase channels corroborate retention/removal but are not substitute equilibrium partition observations. No missing channel was interpreted as zero. Imperfect pre-removal closure is consistent with declared sampling/noise and was preserved rather than forced to unity.

**Limits and testable predictions.** Conclusions apply only to the anonymous categories, phase-ratio range about 0.11–0.59, and tested mixing/settling settings. Reagent and total charged liquid were mostly fixed, so their effects are unavailable. A new S1/X3 condition at intermediate measured phase ratio should approximately follow `O/(O+A) ≈ Dr/(1-r+Dr)` with D near 2.8 as a rough center, but pairing-specific D and impurity/purity changes remain plausible. Independent repeats across the full S×X matrix and separate duration/speed sweeps are needed to resolve interactions and kinetics.

payload.report:
**Account of the behavior**

**Supplied information.** The solvent labels S0–S3 and extractant labels X0–X3 are anonymous, independent benchmark categories; matching suffixes imply no shared identity or property. Consequently, the supplied material catalog supported no polarity-based or molecular explanation. The instrument specification did establish that HPLC measurements made before phase removal were the appropriate evidence for phase ratio and target inventory in each phase, with stated standard deviations of 0.018 for phase ratio and 0.015 for each phase-specific target channel. Final assays were performed only after separation and termination, so they tested what was retained rather than the original partition equilibrium.

**Observations.** At the common baseline recipe and 300 s/600 rpm mixing, material choice produced large changes relative to HPLC uncertainty. With S0, changing X0, X1, X2, and X3 gave organic target inventories of 0.217, 0.404, 0.291, and 0.467 in batches 1–4 (runner-operation-0007, -0017, -0027, and -0037). With X0, changing S0, S1, S2, and S3 gave 0.217, 0.392, 0.310, and 0.429 in batches 1, 5, 6, and 7 (runner-operation-0007, -0047, -0057, and -0067). Thus both supplied-material fields affected partition, and the differences were generally much larger than the 0.015 channel SD.

The S1/X3 phase-amount series was especially diagnostic. The low-organic condition in batch 10 had measured phase ratio 0.109 and aqueous/organic target inventories 0.753/0.258 (runner-operation-0097). Baseline conditions in batches 8 and 12 had ratios 0.178 and 0.195 and inventories 0.582/0.394 and 0.600/0.425 (runner-operation-0077 and -0117). The high-organic condition in batch 9 had ratio 0.594 and inventories 0.218/0.764 (runner-operation-0087). This monotonic response is far larger than measurement uncertainty. Calculating an apparent concentration-partition factor from both inventories and measured phase ratio gives approximately 2.80, 3.12, 2.92, and 2.40 across these conditions.

Mixing evidence was weaker but directionally consistent with incomplete transfer at low contact intensity. Batch 11 used 30 s at 100 rpm and gave organic inventory 0.341 and aqueous inventory 0.652 (runner-operation-0107). The otherwise comparable 300 s/600 rpm batches 8 and 12 gave organic inventories 0.394 and 0.425. The difference exceeds one single-channel SD, although only one weak-mixing run was made and its measured phase ratio also differed.

Phase retention followed the pre-removal measurement rather than a fixed rule. Batches 1–8 and 10–12 retained the aqueous phase because it contained more observed target; batch 9 retained the organic phase because its organic inventory was 0.764 versus 0.218 aqueous. Post-separation final assays corroborated physical removal: batch 9 reported organic target 0.748 and aqueous target 0 after organic retention (runner-operation-0090), while batch 10 reported aqueous target 0.783 and organic target 0.006 after aqueous retention (runner-operation-0100). These final assays do not independently measure the original two-phase partition.

**Inference.** The simplest predictive representation is material-pair-specific preferential partition combined with phase-capacity allocation. For S1/X3, the target concentration appears roughly 2.5–3 times higher in the organic phase after adequate contact, so increasing organic phase share moves a progressively larger fraction of the inventory there. A constant-partition-factor model is a useful first approximation, not an exact law: the inferred factors span about 2.4–3.1. Material effects cannot be reduced safely to separate universal rankings. For example, S1 improved organic inventory relative to S0 when both used X0, but S1/X3 baseline results (0.394 and 0.425) were below S0/X3 (0.467). This suggests pairing dependence, although run variability remains an alternative.

The high-organic S1/X3 batch also showed higher HPLC impurity signal (0.081) and lower purity (0.886) than the low-organic and first baseline runs, which generally had purity near 0.95–0.98. This may indicate a phase-composition tradeoff, but phase amount, composition, and recovery changed together, so it is not established as a separate mechanism.

**Conjecture and competing explanations.** The weak-mixing result may reflect kinetic limitation, but duration and stirring speed were changed simultaneously; altered phase-ratio realization or ordinary batch variability could also explain part of the shift. The apparent variation in partition factor could represent genuine concentration or material interactions, incomplete equilibration, phase-volume measurement error, or noise in two independently measured inventory channels. Imperfect closure of aqueous plus organic signals was retained rather than normalized away.

Scope is limited to these anonymous materials, measured phase ratios of roughly 0.11–0.59, a fixed reagent charge, nearly fixed total charged liquid, and mostly 300 s mixing followed by 300 s settling. Most material-pair cells were measured once, only S1/X3 baseline was repeated, and the full S×X matrix was not sampled. Separate replicated sweeps of mixing duration and speed, repeated material-pair cells, and intermediate phase ratios would be needed to distinguish equilibrium pairing interactions from kinetics and run variability. No real-substance identity or molecular mechanism can be inferred from the supplied anonymous labels.

payload.rationale: I treated the two target fractions as complementary and used the campaign's pre-separation HPLC contrasts to infer material-pair-specific partition preferences, then adjusted allocation for extractant share. S0/X0 favored aqueous at the low Q01 organic volume, while replacing X0 with X3 consistently increased organic allocation, making Q06 exceed Q05. Mixing at 120–1200 s was projected to be near the adequate-contact regime; only a modest penalty was assigned to Q09 and Q11. Intervals are wider for the unmeasured S2/X3 pairing because the campaign showed that solvent–extractant effects were not reliably additive.

payload.report:
1. No instance prior or material-property prior was supplied; the catalog explicitly provided only anonymous labels and said equal suffixes had no shared meaning. The least-tested self-developed law is the transfer of a roughly constant partition factor across material pairs, especially the factorized extrapolation to the unmeasured S2/X3 pair. Batches 8 and 12 supported approximate repeatability for S1/X3, but comparison with batches 1, 4, and 5 showed that solvent and extractant effects were not simply additive. The assumption that all 120–1200 s prediction mixes were effectively equilibrated is also unresolved because batch 11 changed speed and duration together and supplied the only weak-contact result.

2. I would run S2/X3 at the Q08/Q12 material amounts, use strong mixing (600–900 s at 1200 rpm), settle for 300 s, and measure both phase-specific target fractions by HPLC before any phase removal. The factorized partition explanation predicts an organic fraction near 0.74, whereas applying interaction suppression comparable to S1/X3 gives roughly 0.5–0.55. A result near 0.7–0.8 would strengthen transferable solvent/extractant main effects; a result near 0.5 would favor strong pair-specific interaction; a substantially lower or intermediate result would weaken both simple versions and motivate a pair-specific matrix rather than a general material law. One run would not fully distinguish interaction from batch variability, but the proposed predictions differ by much more than the stated HPLC channel noise.

3. The measured phase-ratio channel was underused in the predictions: I largely converted charged volumes directly into phase share, even though the campaign showed variation in measured phase ratio. The paired aqueous and organic readings, their imperfect closure, and the impurity/purity changes—especially batch 9—could also have supported a fuller mass-balance model. Final assays were deliberately used only as retention checks because they occurred after phase removal; using them as equilibrium observations would have been incorrect. Data for X1, X2, and S3 were not relevant to the listed queries but could have informed a hierarchical estimate of between-material variability.

Q08, Q11, and Q12 are least reliable because S2/X3 was never observed; their wide intervals reflect this, but their common high point estimates still rely on the questionable factorization. Q09 and Q11 are additionally weak because the campaign did not separately identify duration and stirring-speed effects. Q01–Q04 also extrapolate the phase-allocation relation beyond the directly observed phase ratio for those exact pairs. The stated 90% intervals were judgmental predictive intervals, not outputs of a fully identified probabilistic model.

There are two tensions between the sealed report and predictions. First, the report emphasized pair interactions, yet the S2/X3 point estimates used an essentially multiplicative main-effect extrapolation; the broad intervals acknowledged but did not eliminate that inconsistency. Second, the report called mixing kinetics unresolved, while the prediction rationale treated most new mixing schedules as near equilibrium and assigned only modest penalties. Finally, the report limited inference to experiments with a fixed reagent charge, whereas the prediction recipes omitted that addition. I did not explicitly propagate uncertainty from that covariate shift; if reagent presence affects partition rather than merely establishing inventory, all twelve predictions are less reliable than their intervals imply.
